ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Persistent dry cough for ~5–6 days with ongoing rhinorrhea.
- Symptoms (onset/duration/severity/aggravating/alleviating): Started ~5–6 days ago; dry, continuous cough that wakes her at night and causes sore throat; associated runny nose; intermittent chills/feeling feverish (no measured temperature); generalized myalgias and marked fatigue/weakness; brief diarrhea at onset that resolved; no shortness of breath at baseline, no chest pain, no ear symptoms, appetite near normal.
- Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypertension.
- Medications/allergies: Metformin; lisinopril. No medication allergies reported.
- Family/social history: Father has type 2 diabetes. Lives with partner (partner currently well). Former smoker (quit ~6 months ago). Drinks wine 2–3 glasses on ~3 evenings/week.
- Vital signs/exam findings: No formal vitals recorded in transcript; exam findings not documented. Patient reports subjective shivering/feeling feverish and muscle aches. No noisy chest or sputum heard by clinician aside from cough.
- Labs/imaging: None mentioned or performed.

V: Pulmonary embolism: Less likely given absence of acute pleuritic chest pain, sudden dyspnea, hemoptysis, or risk-factor change, but can present with cough and malaise in some cases.
I: Viral upper respiratory infection/common cold: Dry cough, rhinorrhea, sore throat from coughing, myalgias and subjective fever/chills, duration ~5–6 days — classic for viral URI.
Acute bronchitis (usually viral): Persistent dry cough that can last days–weeks following an upper respiratory prodrome; nocturnal cough and sleep disturbance fit.
Influenza: Systemic symptoms (chills, myalgias, marked fatigue) with cough and rhinorrhea — could present like this.
COVID-19: Dry cough, myalgias, feverish sensations and transient diarrhea are consistent with COVID-19; partner being well does not exclude it.
N: Lung cancer (central or endobronchial): Would more commonly present with chronic cough over weeks–months and risk factors; unlikely for acute 5–6 day course but considered for persistent cough.
D: Post-viral cough / reactive airways (post-infectious cough): Persistent cough after an acute infection due to airway hyperreactivity — can follow viral URI/bronchitis.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD): Can cause chronic dry cough, but less likely with acute onset and systemic viral symptoms.
I2: ACE inhibitor–induced cough (lisinopril): Classic cause of a dry, persistent cough, often worse at night; relevant because patient is taking lisinopril.
Medication-related side effects or intoxication from other drugs/toxins: Less likely given history.
C: Anatomic/congenital airway abnormality (e.g., tracheomalacia): Unlikely given adult onset and acute course.
A: Allergic rhinitis/post-nasal drip: Rhinorrhea and cough could reflect allergic rhinitis with post-nasal drip causing cough; however systemic symptoms (feverishness, myalgias) argue against a purely allergic cause.
T: Aspiration/foreign body: Unlikely given history and gradual onset; would more likely produce focal symptoms.
E: Thyroid disease (hyperthyroidism): Can cause chronic cough and fatigue but not an acute febrile illness; unlikely for this acute presentation.
Diabetic autonomic dysfunction or metabolic disturbance: Unlikely to explain acute cough and viral symptoms.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Viral upper respiratory infection / acute bronchitis (viral)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: 5–6 day history of rhinorrhea and a continuous dry cough, nocturnal worsening, associated myalgias, subjective fever/chills and transient diarrhea consistent with a viral prodrome. No focal chest signs or severe dyspnea to suggest bacterial pneumonia.
supporting_evidence: Onset ~5–6 days ago with runny nose and dry cough
Cough is continuous and worse at night (typical for bronchitic/post-viral cough)
Associated myalgias, chills/feeling feverish and transient diarrhea consistent with viral illness
No focal chest pain or persistent breathlessness; clinician felt likely viral
opposing_evidence: Cough has already been ongoing for nearly a week — if it persists beyond expected time course, alternative diagnoses should be reconsidered

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Systemic symptoms (shivers/chills, marked myalgias, fatigue) fit influenza; cough and rhinorrhea are also common. Timing and severity (keeping her in bed) are compatible, though no high measured fever or sudden severe onset was documented.
supporting_evidence: Marked fatigue and functional impairment (lying in bed)
Acute onset of cough and rhinorrhea
opposing_evidence: No recorded high temperature or documented abrupt severe onset
Partner is well and patient has been able to attend work some days (though influenza can be mild)
No mention of headache or abrupt onset high fever which often accompany influenza

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Lisinopril is a well-known cause of a dry, persistent cough that is often worse at night. The cough described is dry and nocturnal. However, the acute onset coinciding with other systemic viral symptoms argues more strongly for an infectious cause.
supporting_evidence: Cough is dry and continuous and worse at night, consistent with ACE inhibitor cough characteristics
opposing_evidence: Onset coincided with runny nose, myalgias, chills and transient diarrhea, suggesting an infectious etiology
ACE cough typically lacks systemic symptoms (fever, myalgias, diarrhea)
ACE cough often develops after weeks–months of therapy rather than acutely in a few days (timing unclear in this patient)

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Presentation (dry cough, myalgias, subjective fever/chills, transient diarrhea) is consistent with COVID-19. No test is reported; partner being asymptomatic does not exclude infection.
supporting_evidence: Dry cough with systemic symptoms (myalgias, chills) and transient GI symptom (diarrhea) — all can be seen in COVID-19
Duration of ~5–6 days is compatible with symptomatic COVID-19 course
opposing_evidence: No known exposure reported and partner appears well
No specific symptoms such as loss of taste/smell documented
No testing or objective vital signs to confirm
